Meeting header:
- Date: 2026-05-03
- Time: 09:00 PT / 12:00 ET
- Duration: 49 minutes
- Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Elena Martinez (SE), Kai Nguyen (Redwood Security Engineer); Jordan Lee (CISO), Alex Cho (Identity Lead), Priya Kapoor (Platform Eng), Maya Reynolds (Legal)

Summary:
Quick security and onboarding review focused on SAML/SCIM patterns, least-privilege role mapping, audit logs retention and KMS options. Customer wants clear playbook for test tenant + production cutover and wants to validate data residency + encryption controls before pilot.

Topics covered:
- SSO flow and SAML attributes (NameID, groups, email)
- SCIM provisioning cadence, filters, and group-to-role mappings
- RBAC model: role slices, service accounts, least privilege enforcement
- Audit logs, SIEM export, retention policies and redaction
- Encryption: at-rest, in-flight, CMK vs Redwood-managed keys, rotation
- Data residency and private deployment options

Auto-generated action summary (from call):
- Send SOC2 artifacts and short ISO summary (Samir)
- Draft SCIM mapping and role matrix (Elena)
- Customer to provide IdP attributes and test account (Priya)

Transcript body:
[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone thanks for joining, short agenda today is to run through how we usually do SAML/SCIM onboarding and the least privilege patterns—especially around group sync and audit trails. Jordan, do you want to kick with your success criteria?
[00:22] Jordan: Yeah thanks Samir. For Horizon our big blockers are auditability and key management. We need to know how long logs are kept, how they can be exported to our SIEM, and whether we can use a customer-managed KMS. Timeline is tight, pilot in about three weeks.
[00:40] Alex: Also to add, our identity team wants to avoid heavy manual role mapping. Ideally groups from Okta or Azure map cleanly to roles with minimal transformation.
[00:52] Elena: Totally, we build a role-slice pattern—so you create narrow roles like read-only-embed, gen-internal, admin-console and then map SCIM groups to those. SCIM supports group membership sync; you can scope filters to only provision groups with a prefix, so you don't pull all groups.
[01:15] Priya: Quick Q — our current groups have different naming conventions across teams, will that be problematic?
[01:22] Kai: Not a blocker, we recommend a small normalization step on the IdP or a mapping layer in Redwood. We can accept external group attributes and map them to internal role IDs. Sometimes the transcription here says groupname with a dash, but we support attribute transformations.
[01:45] Alex: How do you handle ephemeral service accounts for automation vs human users?
[01:52] Elena: We suggest separate role slices for service principals. You can issue API keys tied to service roles with scoped permissions and TTLs. For human users, SSO session length + RBAC combine to enforce least privilege.
[02:10] Jordan: Audit logs — what's captured? Full token-level usage?
[02:15] Kai: We collect request metadata, model, route, token counts, user id (if available), and an anonymized text hash. For security-sensitive customers we can turn off full-text retention; instead we store output hashes and metadata only. Logs can be streamed to your SIEM via syslog or S3 with KMS encryption. Retention defaults are 90 days but configurable — we can do 30/90/365 depending on the plan and legal requirements.
[02:45] Maya: Legal will need a data residency statement — where is customer data stored?
[02:50] Samir: Hosted instances operate in specific regions; for EU data we can route to an EU region. For strict residency you may prefer Dedicated or Private deployment which keeps data in your VPC and under your controls. We'll include the region mapping in the playbook.
[03:10] Priya: About KMS — do you support a bring-your-own-key flow?
[03:14] Kai: Yes, we support customer-managed keys (CMK) via standard KMS integrations. For hosted customers we offer both Redwood-managed keys and CMK backed by AWS KMS / GCP KMS / Azure Key Vault. Key rotation is supported, and we perform envelope encryption so raw model weights aren't encrypted by customer KMS but your data blobs are.
[03:38] Jordan: Any SLA implications if we use CMK?
[03:41] Elena: CMK adds a dependency on the KMS availability; we recommend configuring automatic fallback to Redwood-managed keys in case of key access issues, or using dedicated capacity with HSM-backed keys for higher SLAs. We'll document failover behaviors.
[04:00] Alex: Can you walk through a sample SAML attribute mapping?
[04:05] Elena: Sure — typical attributes we consume: NameID (email), email, givenName, familyName, and groups. We prefer groups as an array with a consistent claim name like groups or memberOf. If your IdP uses a different claim name we can map it. Assertion consumer URL and entity IDs are in the metadata we provide; single logout is optional but supported.
[04:30] Priya: Our IdP (Okta) sends groups in a stringified format, sometimes comma separated, can you parse that?
[04:36] Kai: We can add a parsing rule on our side or recommend using Okta transforms. There is a small caveat — if group membership is large (10k+ groups) SCIM performance can degrade; we recommend scoping to a handful of groups that matter to Redwood access.
[04:58] Jordan: SCIM cadence — is it immediate or batched?
[05:02] Elena: SCIM is near-real-time for provisioning changes; we poll or receive changes and sync quickly, but group membership changes might be batched depending on provider rate limits. For Okta we've seen updates within seconds; for Azure AD sometimes a minute.
[05:20] Alex: What about de-provisioning — do user tokens immediately lose access?
[05:24] Kai: We revoke active sessions for the user on de-provision event; tokens issued to long-running jobs (service accounts) will need separate revocation flows — we provide API endpoints to invalidate keys.
[05:40] Priya: For compliance we need an audit trail linking action to an identity. Are actions logged with the original IdP identity?
[05:46] Elena: Yes, audit events include the SSO principal (email or IdP subject). We also include role and request metadata. You can export raw logs to S3 with encryption and then ship to your SIEM.
[06:05] Maya: Regarding PII — is the transcript of prompts stored by default? That's a sensitive area for us.
[06:12] Kai: By default prompts may be retained for quality and evals, but we have options: disable full-text retention, redact PII with tokenization, or store only feature hashes. For customers in regulated industries we configure PII redaction and shorter retention.
[06:36] Jordan: Great. Can we talk about least-privilege patterns? Specifically admin vs dev vs analytics roles.
[06:42] Elena: We recommend the principle of least privilege by splitting responsibilities: admin roles manage configuration and billing; dev roles can create model routes and run jobs; analytics roles can request embeddings but not modify routes. Each role should be designed as the minimal permission set and then you map a small set of SCIM groups to them.
[07:05] Alex: Any tooling to preview effective permissions before rollout?
[07:10] Elena: Yes, the Console includes a simulation mode where you can input a user/group and see effective permissions. We'll include screenshots in the playbook.
[07:22] Priya: If we want to pilot with three teams, what's the recommended rollout?
[07:27] Samir: Pilot pattern we usually use: start with a sandbox project in EU/US region, onboard 1-2 admin users, sync groups for the three teams, validate SCIM provisioning and de-provisioning flows, check audit exports for a week, then cut over production.
[07:45] Jordan: Any red flags or typical gotchas we should watch for?
[07:49] Kai: Common ones — broad admin groups being synced accidentally, forgetting service accounts in de-provision lists, missing group name normalization leading to role mismatches, and KMS policy misconfiguration causing runtime failures. We'll include a checklist to avoid these.
[08:12] Alex: How about multi-tenant data separation? We run multiple product tenants under one Horizon account.
[08:18] Elena: We support tenant scoping at the route and API key level. You can map groups to tenant-scoped roles. For strict separation we'd recommend Dedicated or Private so routing and storage are isolated per tenant.
[08:33] Priya: Do you have SOC 2 and ISO artifacts we can share with procurement?
[08:36] Samir: Yes — I'll share the SOC 2 Type II report, the ISO summary, and a security whitepaper. Those will be sent after the call.
[08:45] Maya: Legal will also ask about subprocessors and subprocessors' locations.
[08:50] Samir: We'll include a subprocessors list and region details in the playbook.
[08:57] Alex: For the SCIM mapping, can you show an example rule for mapping group names to roles?
[09:02] Elena: Example: if group startsWith "rdw-embed-" map to role embed-read; if group contains "admin" map to admin-console (but we strongly recommend avoiding literal admin mapping unless necessary). We'll provide regex examples and a sample CSV you can import.
[09:22] Priya: How do you handle role revocation for long-running asynchronous jobs that request a model mid-run?
[09:30] Kai: For those we recommend service tokens with short TTLs or issuing scoped ephemeral credentials. We also provide an API to revoke tokens; we log the revocation event in the audit trail.
[09:48] Jordan: SIEM integration — we use Splunk. Is there a supported connector?
[09:52] Elena: Splunk via HTTP Event Collector or S3 export works well. We can configure a signed S3 sink with KMS encryption and lifecycle rules that match your retention needs. We'll include a sample Splunk HEC payload.
[10:10] Alex: For the test tenant setup, what are the exact steps we should expect?
[10:14] Samir: Step 1: Exchange SAML metadata and create test IdP app. Step 2: Configure SCIM provisioning to a Redwood test tenant with scoped groups. Step 3: Run basic sanity checks: user login, group sync, role mapping, and audit export. Step 4: Smoke run for API keys and service tokens. We'll provide a checklist.
[10:36] Priya: What's the rollback strategy if a wrong mapping is applied?
[10:40] Kai: We keep change history for mappings and can revert to previous mappings; also the simulation mode helps preview the effect. For immediate rollback we can suspend a mapping and re-evaluate.
[10:55] Alex: Any additional security controls for service accounts?
[11:00] Elena: We recommend mTLS for service traffic in dedicated/private setups, short-lived tokens, and scoped permissions. Review key rotation cadence — we suggest 30/90 day rotation depending on risk level.
[11:20] Jordan: Will you support us in a compliance audit?
[11:24] Samir: Yes we provide an audit package and an engineering contact. For enterprise customers we offer SOC2 review calls and evidence collection.
[11:35] Maya: Can you confirm encryption algorithms used at rest?
[11:38] Kai: We use AES-256-GCM for block storage encryption and TLS1.2+ for in-flight. KMS keys are RSA/ECDSA depending on cloud provider.
[11:50] Alex: A small note — our IdP team prefers sending groups as a claims array rather than SCIM pushing all groups. Which do you prefer?
[11:58] Elena: Either works; group claims are simpler for SAML-only flows, SCIM gives the provisioning state. For provisioning and de-provisioning SCIM is preferable, SAML groups can be used for session claims.
[12:15] Priya: If we disable prompt storage, does that impact model tuning options?
[12:20] Kai: Disabling full-text retention means we won't use prompts for internal evals; we can still collect anonymous metrics for performance. If you want model tuning, we'd need explicit opt-in and contract language.
[12:40] Jordan: Okay let's recap next steps and responsibilities.
[12:44] Samir: I'll send the SOC2 / ISO artifacts and security whitepaper. Elena will prepare the SCIM mapping draft and role matrix. Priya will provide IdP attributes and a test user. We'll aim for the follow-up technical setup call the week of May 11th.
[13:00] Alex: Sounds good, thanks everyone.
[13:05] Maya: Thanks.
[13:10] Samir: Appreciate it, we'll follow up by email with the playbook PDF and checklist.
